drills.q: Walk through the TLS 1.3 handshake message by message.
drills.a: ClientHello (speculative key_share, SNI, ALPN, supported groups) -> ServerHello (server's key_share; both sides derive handshake traffic keys here) -> encrypted EncryptedExtensions, optional CertificateRequest (mTLS only), Certificate, CertificateVerify, Finished from the server -> client replies with its own Certificate/CertificateVerify (mTLS only) and Finished -> application data. 1 RTT total in the common case.

drills.q: Why is TLS 1.3 one round trip faster than TLS 1.2, and what's the cost if the client's key-exchange guess is wrong?
drills.a: TLS 1.2 negotiated cipher/key-exchange choice and then exchanged keys as two sequential round trips; TLS 1.3 speculatively sends a key_share in the first message, collapsing both into one flight. If the server doesn't support that group, it replies with a HelloRetryRequest naming its preferred group, and the client resends -- reverting that connection to effectively 2 RTTs.

drills.q: What did TLS 1.3 remove versus 1.2, and why does each removal matter?
drills.a: Static RSA key exchange (every 1.3 session is now forward-secret by construction), renegotiation (closed the CVE-2009-3555 injection surface, replaced by KeyUpdate for in-session rotation), compression (closed CRIME/BREACH-style side channels), and simplified cipher suites from dozens of TLS 1.2 combinations to 5, all AEAD.

drills.q: Certificate chain validation looks fine at the leaf and root but the connection still fails. What's the most likely cause?
drills.a: An expired or missing intermediate certificate -- the classic real-world cert outage, because monitoring dashboards typically surface only the leaf's expiry, and nobody notices the intermediate needs rotation until validation starts failing across the fleet.

drills.q: What's OCSP stapling and why is it better than a plain OCSP check?
drills.a: Plain OCSP requires the client to call the CA live during the handshake, adding latency and leaking every visited site to that CA, and most clients soft-fail (proceed anyway) if the CA is unreachable -- defeating the point. Stapling has the server periodically fetch a signed OCSP response and attach it to the handshake, so the client verifies freshness locally with no extra network call and no privacy leak.

drills.q: Why is SNI sent in plaintext, and what's the current mitigation?
drills.a: The server needs the hostname to select the right certificate before decryption is even possible, so the ClientHello carrying it necessarily can't be encrypted -- any network observer sees the target hostname. Encrypted ClientHello (ECH) encrypts the real inner ClientHello using a key fetched from DNS (HTTPS/SVCB records), exposing only a generic outer name; deployed by some CDNs (Cloudflare notably) but not yet universal as of mid-2026.

drills.q: Explain ALPN and how HTTP/2 vs HTTP/1.1 actually gets negotiated.
drills.a: ALPN is a ClientHello extension listing the client's supported application protocols in preference order; the server picks one from that list and returns its choice inside the encrypted handshake extensions -- agreement happens as part of the TLS handshake itself, with zero extra round trips, unlike the older cleartext Upgrade: header mechanism used for h2c.

drills.q: What does mTLS add, and how do you roll it out without an outage?
drills.a: The server also sends a CertificateRequest and the client responds with its own Certificate/CertificateVerify/Finished, proving identity cryptographically rather than by network position -- standard for zero-trust service mesh traffic (SPIFFE/SPIRE short-lived certs). Roll out PERMISSIVE (accept both plaintext and mTLS) first, confirm via telemetry that all real traffic is already mTLS, then flip to STRICT; going straight to STRICT breaks any caller not yet onboarded.

drills.q: Session ticket/PSK resumption vs the old session ID mechanism -- what changed and is pure PSK resumption forward-secret?
drills.a: Session IDs required server-side cached state, which doesn't scale across a load-balanced fleet without shared storage. Tickets invert this: the server encrypts its own session state into the ticket itself, so any server sharing the ticket-encryption key can resume with zero stored state. Pure PSK resumption is NOT forward-secret (it reuses original-handshake key material); PSK combined with a fresh (EC)DHE exchange restores forward secrecy at the cost of that extra key exchange.

drills.q: What is 0-RTT, why is it dangerous, and how should a login endpoint that 'looks read-only' be treated?
drills.a: With a valid PSK, a client can send application data in its very first flight before the handshake completes -- genuinely zero round trips. That data isn't protected against replay: a network-positioned attacker can capture and resend it, and the server may process it twice. Mitigation is restricting 0-RTT to strictly idempotent operations. A login endpoint that 'just reads a session' typically still has side effects (rate-limit counters, audit logs, sometimes token issuance), so idempotency must be verified as a property of the actual handler, not assumed from the HTTP verb.

drills.q: You run openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host and get 'Verify return code: 21 (unable to verify the first certificate)'. Diagnose it, and explain why it might pass in Chrome but fail here.
drills.a: Code 21 means the server didn't send a complete chain -- missing intermediate certificate(s) needed to walk up to a trusted root. Fix: serve the full chain file (leaf + intermediates), not just the leaf. Browsers often reconstruct missing intermediates via cached certs or AIA (Authority Information Access) chasing; a bare openssl call or most language HTTP libraries and production services do not, which is exactly the gap that causes 'works in browser, fails in service' incidents.

drills.q: Design the TLS strategy for a service mesh handling both public ingress and internal service-to-service traffic.
drills.a: Public ingress: one-way TLS 1.3 terminated at the edge, ACME-automated cert rotation, OCSP stapling on, 0-RTT disabled or scoped to idempotent GETs only, ECH enabled if supported. Internal: mTLS enforced via the mesh, short-lived (hours) per-workload certs from SPIFFE/SPIRE, rolled out permissive-then-strict, ideally on a separate root of trust from the public chain so a public CA compromise doesn't implicate internal workload identity.

drills.q: A client reports intermittent TLS handshake failures correlating with deploys, and it's not a rotation-atomicity issue -- the cert is identical everywhere. What else could it be?
drills.a: The deploy may have changed the signing CA or intermediate chain itself (not just renewed the same leaf) -- clients or proxies that cached/pinned the old intermediate's public key, or an internal trust store not updated to include the new intermediate, will reject an otherwise-valid new chain even though every node serves it identically.

drills.q: Why does TLS 1.3 mandate ephemeral Diffie-Hellman for every handshake instead of allowing static RSA key exchange as an option?
drills.a: Static RSA key exchange meant a client could encrypt the premaster secret directly with the server's long-term RSA public key; if that private key were ever compromised, every past session recorded off the wire could be decrypted retroactively. Mandating ECDHE makes every session forward-secret by construction -- compromising the server's long-term key doesn't expose past traffic, closing an entire class of 'harvest now, decrypt later' risk that TLS 1.2 left optional.
